sources.name: African Development Bank
sources.text: Press release, "Nigeria Becomes Largest Economy in Africa, with $509.9 Billion GDP" (4 April 2014): the 4 April announcement, $509.9bn against $285.56bn, an 89.2% increase, GDP per capita from $1,437 to $2,688, and Finance Minister Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala's confirmation that the highest global best practices were followed.

sources.name: Financial Times
sources.text: Javier Blas and William Wallis, "Nigeria almost doubles GDP in recalculation" (7 April 2014): analysts' pre-announcement forecasts that rebasing would add 40% to 60%. Paywalled; verified by headline and by matching figures in secondary coverage, not by full-text fetch.

sources.name: Oxford Business Group
sources.text: "Questions raised by Nigeria's recalibrated GDP figures" (2015): the 2-year preparation, the 10-place ranking jump to 26th, and the comparison against South Africa's $354bn.

sources.name: Aluko & Oyebode
sources.text: "How Sustainable is the Effect of Nigeria's GDP Rebasing": the UN Statistical Commission's 5-year recommendation, and the African Development Bank finding on 18 other African countries with base years over a decade old, including the DRC and Equatorial Guinea at over 30 years.

sources.name: Africa Check
sources.text: Factsheet, "Nigeria rebases its economy again: here's what sets it apart" (15 August 2025): the 2025 rebasing from 2010 to 2019, nominal GDP of N372.8 trillion (about $243.3bn) for 2024, a 34.4% increase from about $188bn, Nigeria remaining fourth in Africa, and the University of Benin economist's criticism.

sources.name: Finance in Africa
sources.text: "Inside Nigeria's GDP rebasing" (6 August 2025): the choice of 2019 as a pre-pandemic base year, the Supply and Use Table covering 46 industries and 217 product groups, and the informal economy's 42.5% share.

sources.name: Daily Trust
sources.text: "Rebasing Nigeria's GDP: New Numbers, Old Problems" (August 2025): the debt-to-GDP ratio falling from 52.90% to 39.37% after the 2025 rebasing.
